system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2168-03-27 17:15:00 to 2168-04-06 19:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of recurrent pancreatitis was admitted due to a relapse of severe right epigastric pain shortly after discharge from a prior hospitalization. She was initially kept NPO and managed with IV fluids and a hydromorphone PCA for pain control. Imaging with MRCP showed chronic changes consistent with prior pancreatitis but no acute complications. A PICC line was placed for fluid and medication access, later replaced due to poor flow. Parenteral nutrition was initiated to support nutritional recovery. Her pain improved, allowing transition to oral medications and gradual advancement of diet. Diarrhea was attributed to a new bowel regimen, with negative C. difficile testing. She was discharged home in improved condition with a plan for oral pain management, GI follow-up, and continuation of psychiatric medications.
problems: Other complications due to other vascular device, implant, and graft

You should call your PCP or go to the emergency room if you have 
fevers over 102, chills, worsening abdominal pain, severe nausea 
or vomiting, black or tarry stools or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
AP CHEST ON ___, 11:24 A.M.

HISTORY:  Left PIC.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Left PIC catheter has been withdrawn minimally back to the low SVC.  Lungs
clear.  Heart size normal.  No pleural abnormality or evidence of central
adenopathy.  Findings discussed with the IV nurse earlier in the day.

INDICATION:  Erythema and edema near PICC line.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:  Grayscale and Doppler sonograms of the left internal jugular,
subclavian, axillary, brachial, basilic, and cephalic veins were performed.
Flow is seen throughout the vessels; however, echogenic material is seen
adjacent to the PICC line in the basilic, especially near the elbow.  Findings
are suggestive of a non-occlusive thrombus.

IMPRESSION:  Findings suggesting non-occlusive thrombus in the basilic vein
surrounding the PICC line. Findings discussed with Dr. ___ on ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ female with chronic pancreatitis.  In need of
PICC line for TPN.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___.  Attending radiologist, Dr.
___, was present and supervised the entire procedure.

PROCEDURE/FINDINGS:  Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the right
basilic vein was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set.  Hard copies of the ultrasound images were obtained before
and immediately after establishing intravenous access.  A peel-away sheath was
then placed over a guide wire and a double-lumen PIC line measuring 34 cm in
length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in
SVC under fluoroscopic guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the chest.  The peel-away sheath and guide wire were
then removed.  The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile
dressing applied.  The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no
immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopic-guided double-lumen
PICC line placement via the right basilic vein approach.  Final internal
length is 34 cm with the tip positioned in SVC.  The line is ready to use.

procedures.long_title: Parenteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having that same right upper belly pain again—sharp, goes to my back. It started after I tried eating bread a few days ago. I threw up and the pain got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. You were just discharged a few days ago, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was doing okay on clear liquids, but I thought I could try something soft. Big mistake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with pancreatitis. Your pancreas needs time to heal. For now, we’ll keep you on bowel rest—no food by mouth—to let it rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no eating at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll give you nutrition through an IV. We’re going to place a PICC line to make it easier to give fluids, meds, and eventually, special IV nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had one before. Is it the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, similar. We’ll place it in your left arm today. It’ll help us manage your treatment over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The PICC line was placed yesterday. We’ve started IV fluids and will begin TPN—total parenteral nutrition—tomorrow to support your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a special IV nutrition that gives you calories, protein, and vitamins since you can’t eat. It’ll help you heal and regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My pain is still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re giving you Dilaudid through a PCA pump so you can control the pain safely. We’ll keep adjusting until it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started TPN this morning. Your labs show low potassium, so we’re adding that to your IV. Your lipase is elevated, which confirms the pancreatitis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not uncommon in pancreatitis. We’re watching it closely. We also did an MRCP—special MRI of the pancreas—and it showed chronic changes but no blockages or pseudocysts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blockages? So what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re not sure. Given your family history—your mom had pancreatic cancer—we want to be thorough. We’re ordering a CEA and an endoscopic ultrasound to rule out any small tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s scary. My mom passed from that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your CEA came back normal, which is reassuring. The ultrasound will give us more detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopic ultrasound is done. Good news: no masses or tumors. The pancreas looks mostly normal, with some small cysts, but nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pain is improving too. We’re switching you from the PCA pump to oral Dilaudid. You’ll take it every few hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can start with ice chips and clear liquids. We’ll go slow—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight with clear liquids. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I did throw up once, but not since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on Zofran and Reglan to help with nausea. Your TPN is now running 12 hours a day, so you’ll have some freedom during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, my left arm near the PICC line is red and tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let me take a look. It’s a bit swollen. We’ll get an ultrasound to check for a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows a small non-occlusive clot in the basilic vein near the PICC line. It’s not blocking blood flow, but we’ll remove this line and place a new one in your right arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and not blocking anything. Since it’s related to the catheter, we don’t need blood thinners. But we’ll remove the line to prevent it from growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed the new PICC in your right arm yesterday. It’s working well. Your pain is much better—you’re only taking oral meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel like I can actually breathe again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also stopping your Premarin. Since you had a clot, even a small one, estrogen can increase the risk. You should discuss alternatives with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for years. Are you sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s precautionary. The clot was likely due to the PICC, but estrogen adds risk. We’ll stop it for now and you can talk to your doctor about next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home with the PICC and continue TPN for 12 hours a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who will help me with the TPN at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will come to help with the PICC care and set up the TPN. You’ll also get supplies and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take Dilaudid 2 mg every 2 hours as needed. Don’t take more than prescribed. Call your doctor if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start with clear liquids. Advance slowly—broth, applesauce, toast. If you tolerate it, add soft foods. Avoid fatty or spicy foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the yellow stools I mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely from poor fat digestion due to pancreatitis. We’ll start pancreatic enzyme supplements soon. Your GI doctor will help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. Your vitals are stable, pain is controlled, and you’re tolerating oral meds and ice chips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with prescriptions for pain, nausea, and bowel regimen. Continue omeprazole for your reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visiting nurse will help with daily care—flushing with saline and heparin. Call if you see redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I have pain or vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your PCP or go to the ER if you have fever over 102, worsening pain, severe vomiting, or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep your follow-up with Dr. ___ and your PCP. Take it slow, and don’t rush back to solid foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned my lesson. No bread for a while!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Let your pancreas heal. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a long history of recurrent pancreatitis was readmitted due to a flare triggered by attempting to eat solid food shortly after a prior discharge. She presented with severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, and pain control using a Dilaudid PCA initially, then transitioned to oral hydromorphone. TPN was initiated for nutritional support. An endoscopic ultrasound showed no pancreatic mass, and MRCP revealed only chronic changes. A non-occlusive thrombus was detected near the left PICC line, prompting its removal and placement of a new PICC in the right arm. Estrogen therapy with Premarin was discontinued due to thrombosis risk. She improved clinically, with pain control and tolerance of oral medications, and was discharged home with visiting nurse support for PICC and TPN management, along with follow-up plans.
